title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is training a generative AI system on copyrighted sound recordings without the rights holders' authorization. Udio's model was deployed publicly and attracted millions of users before any licensing arrangements with major labels were in place. The alleged copying happened at the data-ingestion stage, before the model was ever released, which means the problem was baked in from the start and would have required pre-training rights clearance to avoid.

The lawsuits and settlements show three separate legal tracks running at once: UMG settling and moving to a licensing partnership, Warner Music Group doing the same, and Sony Music filing a second lawsuit covering more than 30,000 recordings after a judge blocked those recordings from being added to the original case. A separate class action brought by independent artists was allowed to proceed after a court declined to dismiss it. A musicians' union lawsuit against UMG over the settlement itself adds a further dispute about whether the deal serves artists' interests.

None of the lawsuits have produced a final verdict on liability, and Sony's allegation that Udio copied 30,000 songs is a claim in litigation, not an established finding. What is confirmed is that licensing agreements now exist with at least two major labels and that a new platform using only authorized music is planned, meaning the commercial deployment that preceded those agreements operated outside conditions that the rights holders would have sanctioned.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled its lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model. Under the new licensing agreements, Udio will launch a platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream, and share AI-generated songs. UMG, along with Sony Music and Warner Music Group, had sued Udio for allegedly creating songs similar to copyrighted hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission or compensation. The specific financial terms of the settlement remain undisclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label. Udio's CEO stated the partnership will help unite AI and the music industry while compensating artists who opt into the new platform. Udio, launched in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since its release. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, further demonstrating the growing collaboration between traditional music companies and AI technology firms.
